metadata.title: OpenClaw Evolutionary Coding Lab: a guide to the series
metadata.description: Start here for the bounded coding workflow, its remaining milestone, and eight focused engineering posts.

outcome.summary: Both measured services now use the bounded shared startup-data format. Real custody, startup and altered-record rejection checks pass; production task handling, trusted deployment acceptance and the complete coding demonstration remain unfinished.

provenance.summary: Reorganized from the previously published OpenClaw progress log on September 29, 2026. The engineering snapshot is unchanged; no new experiment is reported here. Engine evidence remains local, and the public source does not independently reproduce its results.

blocks.text: OpenClaw Evolutionary Coding Lab is an experimental, locally operated system for carrying out bounded coding tasks. The intended workflow starts with a task and explicit limits, makes changes in an isolated copy of a project, evaluates the result and returns a patch for human review.

The Lab already has project tracking, planning, task scheduling, reporting and mechanisms that control which actions a task may perform. Development fixtures also exercise parts of the execution system. The current challenge is connecting those components into one demonstrable workflow, including what happens when work fails or is stopped.

This page replaces the expanding progress log with a reading guide. The eight posts below reorganize its published findings by question. They describe the same engineering snapshot; their order is a reading path, not a claim that each experiment happened after the preceding post.

items.label: 1. Reproducible releases: what the tests establish
items.note: separating a repeatable source archive and offline package from a working coding service.

items.label: 2. Stopping work and preserving its outcome
items.note: deadlines, requester loss, durable outcomes, and recovery without replay.

items.label: 3. Connecting tasks, workers and execution evidence
items.note: exact task delivery, native replies, and final-result queries across a real socket.

items.label: 4. Checking runtime records against the bytes they name
items.note: joining source, deployment, service policy and platform evidence without trusting a passing flag.

items.label: 5. Starting the evaluator with measured files and one-use permission
items.note: protected inputs, durable receipts, native parent checks, and the syscall filter that initially stopped Python.

items.label: 6. Starting real services with the files we checked
items.note: service identities, activated sockets, retained files and a connection held before task handling.

items.label: 7. When approval records depend on the program they approve
items.note: removing a circular dependency between measured binaries and deployment acceptance records.

items.label: 8. When realistic runtime data outgrows the startup format
items.note: sharing repeated runtime bytes while preserving role references, limits and rejection checks.

blocks.alt: Intended workflow, with integration still in progress: scope and authorize a task with exact source and limits; claim the attempt once and reject replay; run and evaluate changes in an isolated copy; return the patch and test results for human review while preserving the original project.
blocks.caption: Figure 1. The intended workflow. A complete end-to-end demonstration is still pending.

blocks.text: Measured broker and witness diagnostics run with the shared startup-data format, but their deployment records remain synthetic. Actual accepted deployments, independent peer admission, production request handlers and the original engine's full startup remain unfinished.

The defining milestone is still one bounded coding task in an isolated copy of a project, returning a patch and test results for human review while preserving the original. It must demonstrate success, deliberate failure, replay or restart handling, and cancellation. A passing component test or diagnostic service cannot stand in for that workflow.
The evolutionary part also has a clear limit today. The current convergence process uses a population of one. Broader search across multiple competing candidates remains future work.

sections.title: How future posts will be organized

blocks.text: Each follow-up should answer one engineering question, identify the source state behind the result, describe meaningful failures and state what remains unproven. New milestones belong in a new focused post; this page remains the short entry point and reading guide.
